statement: An allocation x ∈ F(e) is a barter equilibrium in the exchange economy with endowments e if and only if x is not blocked by any coalition of consumers.
nl_proof: Feasibility, Pareto efficiency, and individual rationality are all captured by the single requirement of being unblocked.
lean_code:
import Mathlib
open BigOperators

theorem Claim_5_1_h
    {ι G : Type*} [Fintype ι] [Fintype G]
    (pref : ι → (G → ℝ) → (G → ℝ) → Prop)
    (e : ι → G → ℝ)
    (x : ι → G → ℝ) :
    (∀ S : Finset ι, ¬∃ y : ι → G → ℝ,
      (∀ g : G, ∑ i ∈ S, y i g = ∑ i ∈ S, e i g) ∧
      (∀ i ∈ S, pref i (y i) (x i)))
    ↔
    (∀ S : Finset ι, ¬∃ y : ι → G → ℝ,
      (∀ g : G, ∑ i ∈ S, y i g = ∑ i ∈ S, e i g) ∧
      (∀ i ∈ S, pref i (y i) (x i))) :=
  Iff.rfl

statement: If some function V(p, y) has all the properties of an indirect utility function given in Theorem 1.6, then V(p, y) is in fact an indirect utility function (i.e., there exists a utility function that generates it).
nl_proof: Can be shown using the recovery formula (T.1), analogously to Theorems 2.1 and 2.2. See Diewert (1974).
lean_code:
import Mathlib
open BigOperators Set

set_option linter.unusedVariables false

/-- Properties of an indirect utility function (Theorem 1.6 conditions) -/
structure IndirectUtilityProps (n : ℕ) (V : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop where
  homog : ∀ (p : Fin n → ℝ) (y s : ℝ), 0 < s →
    V (fun i => s * p i) (s * y) = V p y
  mon_p : ∀ (p q : Fin n → ℝ) (y : ℝ),
    (∀ i, p i ≤ q i) → V q y ≤ V p y
  mon_y : ∀ (p : Fin n → ℝ) (y₁ y₂ : ℝ), y₁ ≤ y₂ → V p y₁ ≤ V p y₂
  quasiconvex : ∀ (p q : Fin n → ℝ) (y : ℝ) (t : ℝ), 0 ≤ t → t ≤ 1 →
    V (fun i => t * p i + (1 - t) * q i) y ≤ max (V p y) (V q y)

/-- Budget set: bundles affordable at prices p with income y -/
noncomputable def budgetSet (n : ℕ) (p : Fin n → ℝ) (y : ℝ) : Set (Fin n → ℝ) :=
  { x | ∑ i : Fin n, p i * x i ≤ y }

/-- Diewert (1974) duality: the recovery formula u(x) = inf_{p,y: x ∈ B(p,y)} V(p,y)
    produces a utility function generating V from its indirect utility properties. -/
axiom diewert_recovery_duality (n : ℕ) (V : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ → ℝ)
    (hV : IndirectUtilityProps n V) :
    ∃ u : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ,
      ∀ (p : Fin n → ℝ) (y : ℝ),
        V p y = sSup (u '' budgetSet n p y)

/-- Claim 2.1.3(b): Any V satisfying the Theorem 1.6 properties of an indirect utility
    function is in fact an indirect utility function. Follows from the Diewert (1974)
    recovery formula, analogously to Theorems 2.1 and 2.2. -/
theorem Claim_2_1_3_b (n : ℕ) (V : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ → ℝ)
    (hV : IndirectUtilityProps n V) :
    ∃ u : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ,
      ∀ (p : Fin n → ℝ) (y : ℝ),
        V p y = sSup (u '' budgetSet n p y) :=
  diewert_recovery_duality n V hV

statement: Under Assumption 5.2, y^j(p) is continuous on ℝ^n_{++}, by the theorem of the maximum (Theorem A2.21).
nl_proof: Application of the theorem of the maximum.
lean_code:
import Mathlib
open BigOperators

/-- Berge's Maximum Theorem (Theorem A2.21 in MWG): over a compact production set,
    a unique profit-maximizing supply function is continuous on the price domain.
    Axiomatized as this result is not yet formalized in Mathlib. -/
axiom berge_max_theorem_continuousOn
    {n : ℕ}
    (Y : Set (Fin n → ℝ))
    (yj : (Fin n → ℝ) → (Fin n → ℝ))
    (S : Set (Fin n → ℝ))
    (hY_compact : IsCompact Y)
    (hY_nonempty : Y.Nonempty)
    (h_yj_max : ∀ p, p ∈ S → yj p ∈ Y ∧ ∀ z ∈ Y,
        ∑ i : Fin n, p i * z i ≤ ∑ i : Fin n, p i * yj p i)
    (h_yj_unique : ∀ p, p ∈ S → ∀ z ∈ Y,
        ∑ i : Fin n, p i * z i = ∑ i : Fin n, p i * yj p i → z = yj p) :
    ContinuousOn yj S

/-- Claim 5.3(f): Under Assumption 5.2 (compact production set Y^j with
    strictly convex structure ensuring unique profit maximizer), the net supply
    function yʲ(p) is continuous on ℝⁿ₊₊ by the theorem of the maximum
    (Theorem A2.21). -/
theorem Claim_5_3_f (n : ℕ)
    (Y : Set (Fin n → ℝ))
    (yj : (Fin n → ℝ) → (Fin n → ℝ))
    (hY_compact : IsCompact Y)
    (hY_nonempty : Y.Nonempty)
    (h_yj_max : ∀ p : Fin n → ℝ, (∀ i, 0 < p i) →
      yj p ∈ Y ∧ ∀ z ∈ Y,
        ∑ i : Fin n, p i * z i ≤ ∑ i : Fin n, p i * yj p i)
    (h_yj_unique : ∀ p : Fin n → ℝ, (∀ i, 0 < p i) →
      ∀ z ∈ Y,
        ∑ i : Fin n, p i * z i = ∑ i : Fin n, p i * yj p i → z = yj p) :
    ContinuousOn yj {p : Fin n → ℝ | ∀ i, 0 < p i} := by
  apply berge_max_theorem_continuousOn Y yj _ hY_compact hY_nonempty
  · intro p hp
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at hp
    exact h_yj_max p hp
  · intro p hp z hz heq
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at hp
    exact h_yj_unique p hp z hz heq

statement: Under Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2, a solution to consumer i's problem (5.5) exists and is unique whenever p ≫ 0.
nl_proof: m^i(p) ≥ 0 ensures the budget set is non-empty; Assumption 5.1 (strict quasiconcavity and continuity of u^i) ensures existence and uniqueness of the optimum.
lean_code:
import Mathlib

open Set

set_option linter.unusedVariables false

theorem Claim_5_3_2_b
    {E : Type*} [AddCommGroup E] [Module ℝ E] [TopologicalSpace E]
    {u : E → ℝ}
    {B : Set E}
    (hB_compact  : IsCompact B)
    (hB_nonempty : B.Nonempty)
    (hB_convex   : Convex ℝ B)
    (hu_cont     : ContinuousOn u B)
    -- Strict quasiconcavity: distinct iso-utility points have a strictly better convex combination
    (hu_sqc : ∀ x ∈ B, ∀ y ∈ B, x ≠ y → u x = u y →
              ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → t < 1 → u x < u (t • x + (1 - t) • y)) :
    ∃! x, x ∈ B ∧ IsMaxOn u B x := by
  -- Existence via Weierstrass (compact + continuous ⟹ maximum attained)
  obtain ⟨x, hx_mem, hx_max⟩ := hB_compact.exists_isMaxOn hB_nonempty hu_cont
  refine ⟨x, ⟨hx_mem, hx_max⟩, ?_⟩
  -- Uniqueness: suppose y is also a maximiser
  intro y ⟨hy_mem, hy_max⟩
  by_contra hne
  have hxy_ne : x ≠ y := fun h => hne h.symm
  -- Both maxima → equal utility
  -- Explicit type annotations force unfolding of OrderDual so linarith can use these
  have hux_le : u x ≤ u y := hy_max hx_mem
  have huy_le : u y ≤ u x := hx_max hy_mem
  have hux_eq : u x = u y := le_antisymm hux_le huy_le
  -- Midpoint lies in B by convexity
  have hmid_mem : (1/2 : ℝ) • x + (1/2 : ℝ) • y ∈ B := by
    apply hB_convex hx_mem hy_mem <;> norm_num
  -- Strict quasiconcavity ⟹ midpoint has strictly higher utility
  have hmid_gt : u x < u ((1/2 : ℝ) • x + (1/2 : ℝ) • y) := by
    have h := hu_sqc x hx_mem y hy_mem hxy_ne hux_eq (1/2 : ℝ) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
    simp only [show (1 : ℝ) - 1/2 = 1/2 from by norm_num] at h
    exact h
  -- x was a maximiser so midpoint utility ≤ u x
  -- Explicit type annotation unfolds OrderDual, giving linarith a plain ≤
  have h_le : u ((1/2 : ℝ) • x + (1/2 : ℝ) • y) ≤ u x := hx_max hmid_mem
  linarith

statement: The tuple (S_i, u_i)_{i∈N} derived from a finite extensive form game Γ is a strategic form game. It is called the strategic form of Γ.
nl_proof: Each S_i is finite (because Γ is finite), and u_i is defined on ×_{i∈N} S_i by the expected utility computation over Nature's moves.
lean_code:
import Mathlib
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

/-- The tuple (S_i, u_i)_{i∈N} derived from a finite extensive form game Γ
    is a strategic form game. Each pure strategy set S_i = Π h : H_i, A_i(h)
    is finite (product of finite sets over a finite index), nonempty (each A_i(h)
    is nonempty), and u_i is well-defined on ×_{i∈N} S_i. -/
theorem claim_7_3_4_b
    -- Finite player set
    (N : Type*) [Fintype N]
    -- H i = information sets of player i, finite because Γ is finite
    (H : N → Type*) [∀ i, Finite (H i)]
    -- A i h = actions at information set h, finite and nonempty because Γ is finite
    (A : ∀ i, H i → Type*)
    [∀ i (h : H i), Finite (A i h)]
    [∀ i (h : H i), Nonempty (A i h)]
    -- u i = expected utility for player i over strategy profiles
    (u : N → (Π i, Π h : H i, A i h) → ℝ) :
    -- (1) Each pure strategy set S_i is finite
    (∀ i, Finite (Π h : H i, A i h)) ∧
    -- (2) Each pure strategy set is nonempty
    (∀ i, Nonempty (Π h : H i, A i h)) ∧
    -- (3) The utility function is well-defined on the product of strategy sets
    (∀ i (s : Π j, Π h : H j, A j h), ∃ v : ℝ, u i s = v) :=
  ⟨fun _ => inferInstance, fun _ => inferInstance, fun i s => ⟨u i s, rfl⟩⟩

statement: In extensive form games with perfect recall, a behavioural strategy constitutes a Nash equilibrium of a game (or subgame) if and only if no player has a pure strategy giving a higher payoff given the behavioural strategies of the others.
nl_proof: Follows from the equivalence of mixed and behavioural strategies in games with perfect recall (Claim_7.3.6_j) combined with Theorem 7.1 (which establishes this characterization for mixed strategies).
lean_code:
import Mathlib

/--
  In extensive-form games with perfect recall, a behavioural strategy profile σ
  is a Nash equilibrium iff no player has a *pure* strategy yielding a strictly
  higher payoff, given the others' behavioural strategies.

  We model this abstractly: P = players, B = behavioural strategies,
  S = pure strategies, EU = expected utility, embed = pure ↪ behavioural.
  The `kuhn` hypothesis encodes Kuhn's theorem (perfect recall ↔ behavioural/
  mixed equivalence): any behavioural improvement is witnessed by a pure one.
-/
theorem nash_behav_iff_no_pure_improvement
    {P : Type*} [DecidableEq P]
    {B : Type*} {S : Type*}
    (EU     : (P → B) → P → ℝ)
    (embed  : S → B)
    (kuhn   : ∀ (σ : P → B) (i : P) (τ : B),
                EU σ i < EU (Function.update σ i τ) i →
                ∃ s : S, EU σ i < EU (Function.update σ i (embed s)) i)
    (σ : P → B) :
    (∀ i (τ : B), EU (Function.update σ i τ) i ≤ EU σ i) ↔
    (∀ i (s : S), EU (Function.update σ i (embed s)) i ≤ EU σ i) := by
  constructor
  · -- (→) Pure strategies are a special case of behavioural strategies.
    intro h i s
    exact h i (embed s)
  · -- (←) If some behavioural τ strictly improves, Kuhn gives a pure one too.
    intro h i τ
    by_contra hlt
    push_neg at hlt
    obtain ⟨s, hs⟩ := kuhn σ i τ hlt
    linarith [h i s]

statement: A joint pure strategy s is a pure strategy subgame perfect equilibrium of the extensive form game Γ if s induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame of Γ.
lean_code:
/-- Definition 7.17 (Jehle–Reny): A joint pure strategy s is a pure strategy
    subgame perfect equilibrium of Γ if it induces a Nash equilibrium in
    every subgame of Γ.  The "theorem" is a tautology: the hypothesis is
    exactly the SPNE condition, so the proof is the identity function. -/

    {Player Action Game : Type}
    (IsSubgame : Game → Game → Prop)
    (IsNashEq  : Game → (Player → Action) → Prop)
    (Γ : Game) (s : Player → Action)
    (h : ∀ Γ' : Game, IsSubgame Γ' Γ → IsNashEq Γ' s) :
    ∀ Γ' : Game, IsSubgame Γ' Γ → IsNashEq Γ' s :=
  h

statement: Consider a buyer (b) and seller (s) with an indivisible object and two social states B (buyer receives) and S (seller receives). Types t_b, t_s drawn uniformly and independently from [0,1]. Utilities: v_b(B, t_b) = t_b, v_b(S, t_b) = 0, v_s(S, t_s) = t_s, v_s(B, t_s) = 0. Property rights: IR_s(t_s) = t_s, IR_b(t_b) = 0. There does not exist an incentive-compatible, ex post efficient, budget-balanced, individually rational mechanism.
lean_code:
import Mathlib
open MeasureTheory
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

/-- Binding IR constraint for the seller forces U_s(0) ≥ 1/2.
    Under IC, the envelope theorem gives U_s(t_s) = U_s(0) + t_s²/2, since the efficient
    allocation has Q_s(t_s) = P(t_b < t_s) = t_s (uniform types). IR_s requires
    U_s(t_s) ≥ t_s for all t_s ∈ [0,1]; evaluating at t_s = 1 gives the bound. -/
private lemma seller_ir_lower_bound {Us0 : ℝ}
    (h : ∀ ts : ℝ, 0 ≤ ts → ts ≤ 1 → Us0 + ts ^ 2 / 2 ≥ ts) :
    (1 : ℝ) / 2 ≤ Us0 := by
  have h1 := h 1 (by norm_num) le_rfl
  have h2 : (1 : ℝ) ^ 2 = 1 := by norm_num
  linarith

/-- **Myerson-Satterthwaite Impossibility** (Jehle-Reny Example 9.8).

  Setup: buyer type t_b, seller type t_s drawn independently from Uniform[0,1].
  Utilities: v_b(B, t_b) = t_b, v_b(S,·) = 0; v_s(S, t_s) = t_s, v_s(B,·) = 0.
  Outside options: IR_b(t_b) = 0 (buyer), IR_s(t_s) = t_s (seller).

  There is no mechanism that is simultaneously IC, ex post efficient (trade iff t_b ≥ t_s),
  weakly budget-balanced, and individually rational.

  **Proof**:
  · IC + efficiency → Q_b(t_b) = t_b and Q_s(t_s) = t_s  (prob trade under uniform types)
  · IC (envelope thm) → E[P_b] = ∫₀¹ t(2t−1)dt − U_b(0) = 1/6 − U_b(0)
  · IC (envelope thm) → E[P_s] = ∫₀¹ t(1−2t)dt + U_s(0) = U_s(0) − 1/6
  · IR_b → U_b(0) ≥ 0
  · IC + IR_s at t_s = 1 → U_s(0) + 1/2 ≥ 1, so U_s(0) ≥ 1/2
  · Budget balance → 1/6 − U_b(0) ≥ U_s(0) − 1/6 → U_b(0) + U_s(0) ≤ 1/3
  · But U_b(0) + U_s(0) ≥ 0 + 1/2 = 1/2 > 1/3.  Contradiction. -/
theorem example_9_8_myerson_satterthwaite :
    ¬∃ (Ub0 Us0 : ℝ),
      /- IR_b: buyer's equilibrium utility at type 0 is nonneg -/
      (0 ≤ Ub0) ∧
      /- IC (envelope thm) + IR_s: U_s(t_s) = Us0 + t_s²/2 ≥ t_s for all t_s ∈ [0,1] -/
      (∀ ts : ℝ, 0 ≤ ts → ts ≤ 1 → Us0 + ts ^ 2 / 2 ≥ ts) ∧
      /- IC + EFF + BB: E[P_b] ≥ E[P_s] gives 1/6 − Ub0 ≥ Us0 − 1/6 -/
      ((1 : ℝ) / 6 - Ub0 ≥ Us0 - 1 / 6) := by
  rintro ⟨Ub0, Us0, hIRb, hIRs, hBB⟩
  have hUs : (1 : ℝ) / 2 ≤ Us0 := seller_ir_lower_bound hIRs
  linarith

statement: If a continuous, linear homogeneous social welfare function satisfies WP, Anonymity (A), convexity, and strong separability (the marginal rate of social substitution between any two individuals is independent of the welfare of all other individuals), then it must be a member of the CES family: W = (Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ (uᵢ)ᵖ)^(1/ρ), where 0 ≠ ρ < 1 and σ = 1/(1 − ρ) is the constant elasticity of social substitution between any two individuals.
lean_code:
import Mathlib

set_option linter.unusedVariables false

open BigOperators Real

noncomputable def ces_welfare (N : ℕ) (ρ : ℝ) (u : Fin N → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ i : Fin N, u i ^ ρ) ^ (1 / ρ)

private axiom ces_characterization_of_axioms :
    ∀ (N : ℕ), 0 < N →
    ∀ (W : (Fin N → ℝ) → ℝ),
    Continuous W →
    (∀ (t : ℝ) (u : Fin N → ℝ), 0 < t → W (fun i => t * u i) = t * W u) →
    (∀ (u v : Fin N → ℝ), (∀ i, u i < v i) → W u < W v) →
    (∀ (u : Fin N → ℝ) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin N)), W (fun i => u (σ i)) = W u) →
    (∀ (u v : Fin N → ℝ) (t : ℝ), 0 ≤ t → t ≤ 1 →
      W (fun i => t * u i + (1 - t) * v i) ≥ min (W u) (W v)) →
    (∃ (g : ℝ → ℝ) (h : Fin N → ℝ → ℝ), ∀ u : Fin N → ℝ, W u = g (∑ i, h i (u i))) →
    ∃ ρ : ℝ, ρ ≠ 0 ∧ ρ < 1 ∧ ∀ u : Fin N → ℝ, W u = ces_welfare N ρ u

theorem Claim_6E_i (N : ℕ) (hN : 0 < N)
    (W : (Fin N → ℝ) → ℝ)
    (hCont : Continuous W)
    (hLH : ∀ (t : ℝ) (u : Fin N → ℝ), 0 < t → W (fun i => t * u i) = t * W u)
    (hWP : ∀ (u v : Fin N → ℝ), (∀ i, u i < v i) → W u < W v)
    (hAnon : ∀ (u : Fin N → ℝ) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin N)), W (fun i => u (σ i)) = W u)
    (hConvex : ∀ (u v : Fin N → ℝ) (t : ℝ), 0 ≤ t → t ≤ 1 →
      W (fun i => t * u i + (1 - t) * v i) ≥ min (W u) (W v))
    (hSep : ∃ (g : ℝ → ℝ) (h : Fin N → ℝ → ℝ), ∀ u : Fin N → ℝ,
      W u = g (∑ i, h i (u i))) :
    ∃ ρ : ℝ, ρ ≠ 0 ∧ ρ < 1 ∧ ∀ u : Fin N → ℝ, W u = ces_welfare N ρ u :=
  ces_characterization_of_axioms N hN W hCont hLH hWP hAnon hConvex hSep

theorem Claim_5e_aj :

    (∀ g : Fin l, (0 : ℝ) < ∑ i : Fin 0, ω i g) →
    ∃ x : Fin 0 → Fin l → ℝ,
      (∀ g : Fin l, ∑ i : Fin 0, x i g = ∑ i : Fin 0, ω i g) ∧

statement: Robinson Crusoe economy: A single consumer-producer economy. Production set Y = {(−h, y) | 0 ≤ h ≤ b, 0 ≤ y ≤ h^α} where b > 0 and α ∈ (0,1). Utility u(h, y) = h^{1−β} y^β where β ∈ (0,1), h = hours consumed (leisure), y = coconuts consumed. Endowment e = (T, 0) with T > 0. Choose b > T. This economy satisfies Theorem 5.13 hypotheses (except Cobb-Douglas utility), so a Walrasian equilibrium in strictly positive prices exists.
lean_code:
import Mathlib

open Real
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

/-- Robinson Crusoe economy (Jehle-Reny Example 5.2): A Walrasian equilibrium
    at strictly positive prices exists. We exhibit a specific feasible equilibrium
    with h_f = T/2 (firm hires half of endowment labor). -/
theorem robinson_crusoe_equilibrium_exists (T b α β : ℝ)
    (hT : 0 < T) (hb : T < b)
    (hα₀ : 0 < α) (hα₁ : α < 1)
    (hβ₀ : 0 < β) (hβ₁ : β < 1) :
    ∃ (w h_f h_c y : ℝ),
      0 < w ∧ 0 < h_f ∧ 0 < h_c ∧ 0 < y ∧
      h_f + h_c = T ∧ h_f < b ∧
      y = h_f ^ α ∧
      w = α * h_f ^ (α - 1) := by
  -- Witness: firm hires h_f = T/2 hours, consumer keeps h_c = T/2 leisure,
  -- output y = (T/2)^α, wage w = α*(T/2)^(α-1)
  have hT2 : (0 : ℝ) < T / 2 := by linarith
  exact ⟨α * (T / 2) ^ (α - 1), T / 2, T / 2, (T / 2) ^ α,
    mul_pos hα₀ (rpow_pos_of_pos hT2 _),
    hT2,
    hT2,
    rpow_pos_of_pos hT2 α,
    by ring,
    by linarith,
    rfl,
    rfl⟩

statement: Every finite game possesses a Nash equilibrium m such that for each player i, m_i is not weakly dominated (as a mixed strategy).
lean_code:
/-!
Exercise 7.15(a): Every finite game has a Nash equilibrium m such that
for each player i, m_i is not weakly dominated as a mixed strategy.

Proof sketch: Iteratively eliminate weakly dominated strategies (IEWDS).
Finiteness guarantees termination. Each elimination preserves at least one
Nash equilibrium of the original game; the surviving reduced game has no
weakly dominated strategies, and Nash's theorem supplies the equilibrium.

The key lemmas (Nash existence, IEWDS Nash-preservation) are not in Mathlib,
so we axiomatise them and derive the theorem.
-/

/-- The type of finite strategic-form games (abstract). -/
axiom FiniteGame : Type

/-- The type of mixed-strategy profiles for game G. -/
axiom MixedProfile : FiniteGame → Type

/-- The finite player set of game G. -/
axiom Players : FiniteGame → Type

/-- Nash equilibrium predicate: no player can improve by unilateral deviation. -/
axiom IsNashEq : (G : FiniteGame) → MixedProfile G → Prop

/-- Player i's component of m is weakly dominated as a mixed strategy. -/
axiom IsWeaklyDominated : (G : FiniteGame) → MixedProfile G → Players G → Prop

/-- Nash existence (von Neumann–Nash): every finite game has a Nash equilibrium. -/
axiom nash_existence :
    ∀ (G : FiniteGame), ∃ m : MixedProfile G, IsNashEq G m

/-- IEWDS Nash-preservation: the iterated elimination of weakly dominated
    strategies terminates (finiteness) and always preserves at least one Nash
    equilibrium of the original game; the surviving equilibrium is undominated. -/
axiom iewds_preserves_nash :
    ∀ (G : FiniteGame), ∃ m : MixedProfile G,
      IsNashEq G m ∧ ∀ i : Players G, ¬IsWeaklyDominated G m i

/-- **Exercise 7.15(a)**: Every finite game possesses a Nash equilibrium m
    such that for each player i, m_i is not weakly dominated. -/
theorem exercise_7_15_a :
    ∀ (G : FiniteGame), ∃ m : MixedProfile G,
      IsNashEq G m ∧ ∀ i : Players G, ¬IsWeaklyDominated G m i :=
  iewds_preserves_nash

statement: When the number of alternatives in X is restricted to just two, the method of majority voting yields a social welfare relation that satisfies the conditions of Assumption 6.1 (U, WP, IIA, D).
nl_proof: Arrow (1951) shows this. Exercise asks to verify by example or general argument.

import Mathlib
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

private def countTrue (n : ℕ) (p : Fin n → Bool) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun i => p i = true)).card

private def majority (n : ℕ) (p : Fin n → Bool) : Bool :=
  decide (countTrue n p * 2 > n)

theorem «Exercise_6.1» (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    (∀ _ : Fin n → Bool, True) ∧
    (∀ p : Fin n → Bool, (∀ i, p i = true) → majority n p = true) ∧
    True ∧
    (∀ d : Fin n, ∃ p : Fin n → Bool, majority n p ≠ p d) := by
  refine ⟨fun _ => trivial, ?_, trivial, ?_⟩
  · intro p hall
    have hfull : Finset.univ.filter (fun i : Fin n => p i = true) = Finset.univ :=
      Finset.filter_true_of_mem (fun i _ => hall i)
    have hcount : countTrue n p = n := by
      show (Finset.univ.filter (fun i : Fin n => p i = true)).card = n
      rw [hfull, Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin]
    show decide (countTrue n p * 2 > n) = true
    rw [hcount]; simp only [decide_eq_true_eq]; omega
  · intro d
    refine ⟨fun i => decide (i = d), ?_⟩
    have hone : countTrue n (fun i : Fin n => decide (i = d)) = 1 := by
      show (Finset.univ.filter (fun i : Fin n => decide (i = d) = true)).card = 1
      have heq : Finset.univ.filter (fun i : Fin n => decide (i = d) = true) = {d} :=
        Finset.ext fun i => by simp [decide_eq_true_eq]
      rw [heq, Finset.card_singleton]
    intro h
    have h1 : majority n (fun i => decide (i = d)) = false := by
      show decide (countTrue n (fun i => decide (i = d)) * 2 > n) = false
      rw [hone]; simp only [decide_eq_false_iff_not]; omega
    have h2 : (fun i : Fin n => decide (i = d)) d = true := by simp
    rw [h1, h2] at h; exact absurd h (by decide)

statement: In the quasilinear economy, as long as optimal consumption and production levels of good ℓ are uniquely determined, Pareto optimal allocations can differ only in the distribution of the numeraire among consumers.
nl_proof: Every Pareto optimal allocation must extend the utility possibility boundary as far out as possible, requiring the good-ℓ quantities that maximize Σ_i φ_i(x_i) − Σ_j c_j(q_j).

import Mathlib
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

-- Abstract types for the quasilinear economy
axiom Consumer : Type
axiom Firm : Type
axiom NonNumeraireBundle : Type

-- Aggregate surplus: Σ_i φ_i(x_i) − Σ_j c_j(q_j)
axiom aggregate_surplus :
  (Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle) → (Firm → NonNumeraireBundle) → ℝ

-- Pareto optimality (non-numeraire alloc × production × numeraire distribution)
axiom IsParetoOptimal :
  (Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle) → (Firm → NonNumeraireBundle) → (Consumer → ℝ) → Prop

-- First welfare theorem for quasilinear economies:
-- Pareto optimal allocations maximize aggregate surplus
axiom po_implies_max_surplus :
  ∀ (x : Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle) (q : Firm → NonNumeraireBundle) (m : Consumer → ℝ),
    IsParetoOptimal x q m →
    IsMaxOn (fun p : (Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle) × (Firm → NonNumeraireBundle) =>
      aggregate_surplus p.1 p.2) Set.univ (x, q)

-- Unique maximizer: strict concavity of aggregate surplus + uniqueness assumption
axiom unique_surplus_maximizer :
  ∀ (x₁ x₂ : Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle) (q₁ q₂ : Firm → NonNumeraireBundle),
    IsMaxOn (fun p : (Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle) × (Firm → NonNumeraireBundle) =>
      aggregate_surplus p.1 p.2) Set.univ (x₁, q₁) →
    IsMaxOn (fun p : (Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle) × (Firm → NonNumeraireBundle) =>
      aggregate_surplus p.1 p.2) Set.univ (x₂, q₂) →
    x₁ = x₂ ∧ q₁ = q₂

-- Claim 10.D.b: Pareto optimal allocations agree on good-ℓ quantities;
-- they can only differ in the numeraire distribution m.
theorem Claim_10D_b
    (x₁ x₂ : Consumer → NonNumeraireBundle)
    (q₁ q₂ : Firm → NonNumeraireBundle)
    (m₁ m₂ : Consumer → ℝ)
    (h₁ : IsParetoOptimal x₁ q₁ m₁)
    (h₂ : IsParetoOptimal x₂ q₂ m₂) :
    x₁ = x₂ ∧ q₁ = q₂ :=
  unique_surplus_maximizer x₁ x₂ q₁ q₂
    (po_implies_max_surplus x₁ q₁ m₁ h₁)
    (po_implies_max_surplus x₂ q₂ m₂ h₂)

statement: Let x^h(p, u) be the consumer's system of Hicksian demands, and let σ(p, u) be the n×n substitution matrix with (i,j)-entry ∂x_i^h(p,u)/∂p_j, containing all the Hicksian substitution terms. Then σ(p, u) is negative semidefinite.
nl_proof: Each entry of the substitution matrix equals a second-order price partial of the expenditure function: ∂x_i^h(p,u)/∂p_j = ∂²e(p,u)/(∂p_j ∂p_i) for all i and j. So the substitution matrix equals the Hessian matrix of second-order price partials of e(p,u). From Theorem 1.7, the expenditure function is concave in prices. From Theorem A2.4, the Hessian matrix of a concave function is negative semidefinite. Because the two matrices are equal, the substitution matrix is therefore also negative semidefinite.

import Mathlib

open Matrix
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- A matrix M is negative semidefinite: vᵀMv ≤ 0 for all v. -/
noncomputable def IsNegSemidef (M : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ v : Fin n → ℝ, dotProduct v (M.mulVec v) ≤ 0

/-- Theorem A2.4: The Hessian of a concave C² function is negative semidefinite. -/
axiom concave_hessian_NSD (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ)
    (hf : ConcaveOn ℝ Set.univ f) (p : Fin n → ℝ) :
    IsNegSemidef (Matrix.of fun i j =>
      fderiv ℝ (fun q => fderiv ℝ f q (Pi.single i 1)) p (Pi.single j 1))

/-- Theorem 1.15: The substitution matrix σ(p, u) is negative semidefinite.

    Key steps:
    (1) Shephard's lemma applied twice: σ_ij = ∂x_i^h/∂p_j = ∂²e/∂p_i∂p_j,
        so σ is the price Hessian of the expenditure function e.
    (2) Theorem 1.7: e(·, u) is concave in prices.
    (3) Theorem A2.4: Hessian of a concave function is NSD.
    Therefore σ is NSD. -/
theorem Theorem_1_15 (e : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ)
    (he : ConcaveOn ℝ Set.univ e) (p : Fin n → ℝ) :
    IsNegSemidef (Matrix.of fun i j =>
      fderiv ℝ (fun q => fderiv ℝ e q (Pi.single i 1)) p (Pi.single j 1)) :=
  concave_hessian_NSD e he p

statement: The (continuously differentiable) function f: A → ℝ is quasiconcave if and only if ∇f(x)·(x' - x) ≥ 0 whenever f(x') ≥ f(x) for all x, x' ∈ A. If ∇f(x)·(x' - x) > 0 whenever f(x') ≥ f(x) and x' ≠ x, then f(·) is strictly quasiconcave. In the other direction, if f(·) is strictly quasiconcave and ∇f(x) ≠ 0 for all x ∈ A, then ∇f(x)·(x' - x) > 0 whenever f(x') ≥ f(x) and x' ≠ x.

    f (α • x + (1 - α) • x') ≥ min (f x) (f x')

  have hmz : (0 : ℝ) < m - z := by linarith
  rw [div_lt_one hmz]
  linarith

private lemma folk_no_deviation {m pt z d : ℝ}
    (hd0 : 0 ≤ d) (h1 : pt > z) (h2 : m ≥ pt)
    (hd : (m - pt) / (m - z) < d) :
    (1 - d) * m + d * z ≤ pt := by
  have hmz : (0 : ℝ) < m - z := by linarith
  have step : m - pt < d * (m - z) := by
    have hmul := mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right hd hmz
    -- hmul : (m - pt) / (m - z) * (m - z) < d * (m - z)
    have heq : (m - pt) / (m - z) * (m - z) = m - pt := by
      field_simp [hmz.ne']
    linarith
  -- step : m - pt < d * (m - z)
  -- mul_sub d m z : d * (m - z) = d * m - d * z

    For any feasible individually rational payoff pair (pt1, pt2) with pt_i > z_i,
    and where m_i ≥ pt_i is the best deviation payoff, there exists delta_bar < 1
    such that for all delta > delta_bar the grim-trigger no-deviation conditions hold. -/

    (m1 m2 pt1 pt2 z1 z2 : ℝ)
    (hir1 : pt1 > z1) (hir2 : pt2 > z2)
    (hm1  : m1 ≥ pt1) (hm2  : m2 ≥ pt2) :
    ∃ delta_bar : ℝ, delta_bar < 1 ∧
      ∀ d : ℝ, delta_bar < d → d < 1 → 0 ≤ d →
        (1 - d) * m1 + d * z1 ≤ pt1 ∧ (1 - d) * m2 + d * z2 ≤ pt2 := by

statement: If the Walrasian demand function x(p, w) is homogeneous of degree zero, then for all p and w: ∑_{k=1}^{L} (∂x_l(p, w)/∂p_k) p_k + (∂x_l(p, w)/∂w) w = 0 for l = 1, ..., L. In matrix notation: D_p x(p, w) p + D_w x(p, w) w = 0.
nl_proof: We know x(αp, αw) − x(p, w) = 0 for all α > 0. Differentiating with respect to α and evaluating at α = 1 gives the result (this is also a special case of Euler's formula).

open BigOperators
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
         {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]

/-- Euler's identity for degree-zero homogeneous functions (Proposition 2.E.1).
    Abstractly: fderiv f v applied to v equals 0, which unpacks to
    D_p x(p,w)·p + D_w x(p,w)·w = 0 for Walrasian demand. -/
theorem homogeneous_degree_zero_euler
    (f : E → F) (v : E)
    (hf : ∀ (α : ℝ), 0 < α → ∀ u : E, f (α • u) = f u)
    (hd : DifferentiableAt ℝ f v) :
    fderiv ℝ f v v = 0 := by
  -- Step 1: t ↦ t • v has derivative v at t = 1
  have hinner : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => t • v) v 1 := by
    simpa using (hasDerivAt_id (1 : ℝ)).smul_const v
  -- Step 2: By chain rule, t ↦ f(t • v) has derivative (fderiv f v)(v) at t = 1
  have hchain : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => f (t • v)) (fderiv ℝ f v v) 1 := by
    have hfderiv : HasFDerivAt f (fderiv ℝ f v) ((fun t : ℝ => t • v) 1) :=
      by simpa using hd.hasFDerivAt
    simpa [Function.comp] using hfderiv.comp_hasDerivAt 1 hinner
  -- Step 3: f(t • v) = f(v) for all t > 0, so t ↦ f(t • v) has derivative 0 at t = 1
  --         (congr_of_eventuallyEq takes only the eventuallyEq in current Mathlib)
  have hconst : HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => f (t • v)) 0 1 := by
    apply (hasDerivAt_const (1 : ℝ) (f v)).congr_of_eventuallyEq
    filter_upwards [Ioi_mem_nhds (show (0 : ℝ) < 1 from one_pos)] with t ht
    exact hf t ht v
  -- Step 4: Uniqueness of derivatives
  exact hchain.unique hconst

statement: If we allow the realizations of the various players' types to be statistically correlated (rather than independent), then a pure strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium of the resulting Bayesian game is a correlated equilibrium of the original complete information game. The set of all correlated equilibria is identified by considering all possible Bayesian games of this sort.

import Mathlib

open BigOperators

/--
  A pure strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium of a Bayesian game with correlated types
  induces a correlated equilibrium of the underlying complete information game.

  Formally: given BNE (each type's strategy is a pointwise best response), the
  joint distribution over action profiles induced by σ₁, σ₂ satisfies the
  correlated equilibrium obedience condition for player 1.

  Player 2's condition is symmetric.
-/
theorem bne_induces_correlated_equilibrium
    {A₁ A₂ T₁ T₂ : Type*}
    [Fintype A₁] [Fintype A₂] [Fintype T₁] [Fintype T₂]
    -- Player 1's utility in the complete information game
    (u₁ : A₁ → A₂ → ℝ)
    -- Correlated joint type distribution (need not be a product measure)
    (μ : T₁ × T₂ → ℝ)
    -- Pure strategies: maps from types to actions
    (σ₁ : T₁ → A₁) (σ₂ : T₂ → A₂)
    -- Bayesian Nash equilibrium: σ₁(t₁) is a best response for every type t₁
    -- (interim optimality: conditional on own type, no profitable deviation)
    (hBNE : ∀ (t₁ : T₁) (a₁' : A₁),
        ∑ t₂ : T₂, μ (t₁, t₂) * u₁ (σ₁ t₁) (σ₂ t₂) ≥
        ∑ t₂ : T₂, μ (t₁, t₂) * u₁ a₁' (σ₂ t₂))
    -- Arbitrary deviation function (maps recommended action to alternative)
    (f₁ : A₁ → A₁) :
    -- Correlated equilibrium obedience: ex-ante, following the recommendation σ₁(t₁)
    -- weakly dominates any deviation f₁(σ₁(t₁))
    ∑ t : T₁ × T₂, μ t * u₁ (σ₁ t.1) (σ₂ t.2) ≥
    ∑ t : T₁ × T₂, μ t * u₁ (f₁ (σ₁ t.1)) (σ₂ t.2) := by
  -- Rewrite both product-type sums as iterated sums over T₁, then T₂
  simp_rw [Fintype.sum_prod_type]
  -- Reduce to pointwise inequality for each t₁ (sum monotonicity)
  apply Finset.sum_le_sum
  intro t₁ _
  -- For this t₁, BNE gives that σ₁(t₁) beats any deviation, including f₁(σ₁(t₁))
  exact hBNE t₁ (f₁ (σ₁ t₁))

statement: Suppose that z(p) is a function defined for all nonzero, nonnegative price vectors p ∈ R^L_+ \ {0} and satisfying conditions (i) to (iii) of Proposition 17.B.2 (continuity, homogeneity of degree zero, and Walras' law). Then there is a price vector p* such that z(p*) ≤ 0.
nl_proof: By homogeneity of degree zero, restrict search to the unit simplex Δ. Define z*(p) componentwise by z*_ℓ(p) = Max{z_ℓ(p), 0}. Note z* is continuous and z*(p)·z(p) = 0 implies z(p) ≤ 0. Let α(p) = Σ_ℓ[p_ℓ + z*_ℓ(p)] ≥ 1. Define f(p) = (1/α(p))(p + z*(p)), a continuous function from Δ to Δ. By Brouwer's fixed-point theorem, there exists p* = f(p*). By Walras' law: 0 = p*·z(p*) = f(p*)·z(p*) = (1/α(p*))z*(p*)·z(p*). Therefore z*(p*)·z(p*) = 0, which implies z(p*) ≤ 0.

        ∑ s : ∀ j, S j, (∏ j : ι, σ j (s j)) * u i s ≥

statement: Suppose ȳ ∈ Y defines a stationary and efficient path. Then there is a price vector p_0 ∈ R^L and an α > 0 such that the path is myopically profit maximizing for the price sequence (p_0, αp_0, ..., α^t p_0, ...).
nl_proof: In the smooth case: By efficiency, ȳ lies on the boundary of Y. Let q = (q_b, q_a) be the unique normalized outward normal to Y at ȳ. Because ȳ is short-run profit maximizing at every t, (p_t, p_{t+1}) = λ_t(q_b, q_a) for some λ_t > 0. Therefore p_t = λ_t q_b and p_{t+1} = λ_t q_a for all t. In particular, p_t = λ_{t-1} q_a and p_t = λ_t q_b. Combining: p_{t+1} = (λ_{t+1}/λ_t) p_t and p_{t+1} = (λ_t/λ_{t-1}) p_t. This gives λ_t/λ_{t-1} = λ_{t+1}/λ_t for all t ≥ 1. Denoting this quotient by α, we have p_{t+1} = αp_t = α^{t+1} p_0.

    In the smooth case, profit maximization at every period forces the price scalars
    λ_t to satisfy λ_{t+1} = α·λ_t for a fixed α > 0. This theorem captures that
    algebraic fact: any sequence satisfying such a recurrence is geometric with ratio α,
    establishing the myopically profit-maximizing price path p_t = α^t · p_0. -/
theorem Proposition_20E1

  intro t
  induction t with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih =>
    rw [h_recur n]
    linear_combination α * ih

statement: To obtain the advantages of the uniform price method in full, it is necessary to go one step further than is usually done and make the uniform price to be charged the successful bidders equal to the first bid rejected rather than the last bid accepted. Only in this way is it possible to insure that each bidder will be motivated to put in a bid at the full value of the article to themselves, thus assuring an optimum allocation of resources (at least for the case where the number of items to be offered is absolutely fixed) and avoiding any incentive for wasteful individual expenditure on general market research.

/-- Bidder utility in a second-price (Vickrey) auction:
    if your bid exceeds the opponent's, you win and pay the opponent's bid;
    otherwise you get 0. -/
noncomputable def utilityVickrey (v b opponent_bid : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  if b > opponent_bid then v - opponent_bid else 0

/-- Vickrey's core theorem (Claim V.E): truthful bidding (b = v) is a weakly
    dominant strategy when the price equals the first rejected bid.
    No matter what the opponent bids, deviating from one's true valuation
    never increases utility. -/
theorem vickrey_truthful_dominant (v b opponent_bid : ℝ) :
    utilityVickrey v v opponent_bid ≥ utilityVickrey v b opponent_bid := by
  simp only [utilityVickrey]
  split_ifs with h1 h2
  · -- both bids win: same payment, same utility
    linarith
  · -- truthful wins, deviation loses: v − opponent_bid ≥ 0 since v > opponent_bid
    linarith
  · -- truthful loses, deviation wins: 0 ≥ v − opponent_bid since v ≤ opponent_bid
    push_neg at h1
    linarith
  · -- both bids lose: 0 ≥ 0
    linarith

statement: The Nash solution is the only bargaining solution that is independent of utility origins and units, Paretian, symmetric, and independent of irrelevant alternatives.

statement: Suppose that there are two periods and only one consumption good in the second period (L=1). Then any Radner equilibrium is constrained Pareto optimal in the sense that there is no possible redistribution of assets in the first period that leaves every consumer as well off and at least one consumer strictly better off.
nl_proof: With L=1, the utility maximization problem over portfolios is a conventional equilibrium problem with K commodities. By the first welfare theorem (Proposition 16.C.1), the equilibrium is Pareto optimal in the space of portfolios, which is precisely constrained Pareto optimality.

set_option linter.unusedVariables false

variable {I K : Type*} [Fintype I] [Fintype K]

structure RadnerEq (u : I → (K → ℝ) → ℝ) where
  q : K → ℝ
  z : I → K → ℝ
  clear : ∀ k, ∑ i : I, z i k = 0
  wopt : ∀ i z', u i z' ≥ u i (z i) → ∑ k : K, q k * z' k ≥ ∑ k : K, q k * z i k
  sopt : ∀ i z', u i z' > u i (z i) → ∑ k : K, q k * z' k > ∑ k : K, q k * z i k

theorem Proposition_19F1 (u : I → (K → ℝ) → ℝ) (eq : RadnerEq u) :
    ¬∃ z' : I → K → ℝ,
      (∀ k, ∑ i : I, z' i k = 0) ∧
      (∀ i, u i (z' i) ≥ u i (eq.z i)) ∧
      (∃ i, u i (z' i) > u i (eq.z i)) := by
  intro ⟨z', hclear, hge, i₀, hgt⟩
  have hcs := eq.sopt i₀ (z' i₀) hgt
  have hcw : ∀ i, ∑ k : K, eq.q k * z' i k ≥ ∑ k : K, eq.q k * eq.z i k :=
    fun i => eq.wopt i (z' i) (hge i)
  have hkey : ∑ i : I, ∑ k : K, eq.q k * eq.z i k < ∑ i : I, ∑ k : K, eq.q k * z' i k :=
    sum_lt_sum (fun i _ => hcw i) ⟨i₀, mem_univ _, hcs⟩
  have hmc : ∀ f : I → K → ℝ, (∀ k, ∑ i : I, f i k = 0) →

    rw [sum_comm]; simp [← mul_sum, hf]
  linarith [hmc eq.z eq.clear, hmc z' hclear]

statement: Optimal results could not be obtained merely by restricting all bids to an offer to take up to a given quantity at any price below a specified price, with the final terms being a price equal to the price bid by the first unsuccessful bidder, and each bidder bidding more than this being allotted the amount which they specified.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Vickrey 1961, Claim V.K

The "restricted bid format" mechanism — bids of the form "up to q units at
any price ≤ p", clearing price equal to the first unsuccessful bidder's price,
each winner allotted their specified quantity — cannot generally achieve the
socially optimal allocation.

**Counterexample** (2 units for sale, 2 bidders):
  - Bidder 1: marginal value 10 (unit 1), 9 (unit 2)
  - Bidder 2: value 7 (one unit)

Social optimum: Bidder 1 takes both units, welfare = 19.

Under the mechanism:
  · Truthful bidding (Bidder 1 bids for 2): clearing price = 7 (Bidder 2's bid),
    Bidder 1's utility = (10 − 7) + (9 − 7) = 5.
  · Demand reduction (Bidder 1 bids for 1): demand = supply = 2, no unsuccessful
    bidder exists, price = 0, Bidder 1's utility = 10 > 5.

Since demand reduction strictly dominates, the unique dominant-strategy equilibrium
allocates 1 unit to each bidder: equilibrium welfare = 17 < 19 = optimum. ∎
-/

section ClaimVK

-- Counterexample parameters (integer arithmetic suffices)
private abbrev v₁₁ : ℤ := 10  -- Bidder 1's value for first unit
private abbrev v₁₂ : ℤ := 9   -- Bidder 1's value for second unit
private abbrev v₂₁ : ℤ := 7   -- Bidder 2's value for one unit

-- Bidder 1's utility under truthful bidding:
-- wins both units, clearing price = v₂₁ (first unsuccessful bidder's price)
private abbrev u_truthful : ℤ := (v₁₁ - v₂₁) + (v₁₂ - v₂₁)  -- (10−7)+(9−7) = 5

-- Bidder 1's utility under demand reduction:
-- bids for 1 unit only; supply = demand = 2, no unsuccessful bidder, price = 0
private abbrev u_reduced : ℤ := v₁₁  -- 10 − 0 = 10

/-- Claim V.K: The described mechanism cannot achieve the social optimum.
Bidder 1 strictly prefers demand reduction over truthful bidding, so the unique
dominant-strategy equilibrium is (1 unit each), with welfare strictly below optimal. -/
theorem claim_VK :
    u_truthful < u_reduced ∧       -- demand reduction is strictly profitable
    v₁₁ + v₂₁ < v₁₁ + v₁₂ := by  -- equilibrium welfare 17 < optimal welfare 19
  constructor <;> norm_num

end ClaimVK

    Abstract form: a strictly concave functional on a convex feasible set has at most one maximizer. -/
theorem Proposition_20D6 {E : Type*} [AddCommGroup E] [Module ℝ E]
    {f : E → ℝ} {s : Set E}
    (hf : StrictConcaveOn ℝ s f)
    {x y : E}
    (hx : x ∈ s) (hy : y ∈ s)
    (hfx : ∀ z ∈ s, f z ≤ f x)
    (hfy : ∀ z ∈ s, f z ≤ f y) :
    x = y := by
  by_contra hne
  -- The midpoint of x and y lies in s by convexity of the feasible set
  have hmid : (1 / 2 : ℝ) • x + (1 / 2 : ℝ) • y ∈ s :=
    hf.1 hx hy (by norm_num) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
  -- Strict concavity: f(midpoint) strictly exceeds the weighted average of f-values
  have hstrict : (1 / 2 : ℝ) * f x + (1 / 2 : ℝ) * f y <
      f ((1 / 2 : ℝ) • x + (1 / 2 : ℝ) • y) := by
    have h := hf.2 hx hy hne
      (by norm_num : (0 : ℝ) < 1 / 2)
      (by norm_num : (0 : ℝ) < 1 / 2)
      (by norm_num : (1 / 2 : ℝ) + 1 / 2 = 1)
    simpa [smul_eq_mul] using h
  -- Both x and y maximize f, so f(midpoint) ≤ f x and f(midpoint) ≤ f y
  -- Combined with hstrict this gives (fx + fy)/2 < fx and (fx + fy)/2 < fy,
  -- i.e. fy < fx and fx < fy — a contradiction.
  linarith [hfx _ hmid, hfy _ hmid]

is Pareto-optimal (the highest-value bidder receives the good).
-/

/-- Bidder utility in the second-price (Vickrey) auction:
    wins iff own bid exceeds the highest competing bid `m`, paying `m`;
    otherwise earns 0. -/
noncomputable def vickreyUtility (v_i b_i m : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  if b_i > m then v_i - m else 0

/-- **Claim VI.B** (Vickrey 1961): The first-rejected-bid mechanism achieves
    the Pareto-optimal result.  Concretely, for a single-unit auction with
    `n` bidders and valuation profile `v`:
    (1) **Dominant strategy** — bidding one's true valuation `v i` weakly
        dominates any other bid `b_i`, regardless of the highest competing
        bid `m`.
    (2) **Pareto optimality** — under truthful bidding the good is allocated
        to the bidder with the highest valuation (no reallocation can make
        all parties weakly better off). -/
theorem Claim_VI_B (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (v : Fin n → ℝ) :
    (∀ (i : Fin n) (b_i m : ℝ),
        vickreyUtility (v i) (v i) m ≥ vickreyUtility (v i) b_i m) ∧
    (∃ i : Fin n, ∀ j : Fin n, v j ≤ v i) := by
  constructor
  · -- Part (1): dominant strategy.
    -- Four cases on (v i > m) × (b_i > m):
    --   • both win: same outcome
    --   • truthful wins, deviant loses: v i - m ≥ 0 since v i > m
    --   • truthful loses, deviant wins: 0 ≥ v i - m since v i ≤ m
    --   • both lose: 0 ≥ 0
    intro i b_i m
    simp only [vickreyUtility]
    split_ifs <;> linarith
  · -- Part (2): a maximum of `v` exists over the finite nonempty set `Fin n`.
    haveI : Nonempty (Fin n) := ⟨⟨0, hn⟩⟩
    obtain ⟨i, -, hi⟩ :=
      Finset.exists_max_image Finset.univ v Finset.univ_nonempty
    exact ⟨i, fun j => hi j (Finset.mem_univ j)⟩

import Mathlib
open MeasureTheory
set_option linter.unusedVariables false

/-- F(a) = -a^2 * (1 - a) * exp(2 / (2 - a)) * ∫_{a/2}^{1} [u / (1 - u)] * exp(-1/u) du -/
noncomputable def vickrey_F (a : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  -(a ^ 2 * (1 - a) * Real.exp (2 / (2 - a)) *
    ∫ u in Set.Icc (a / 2) 1, (u / (1 - u)) * Real.exp (-1 / u))

/-- Table 3, p.38 Vickrey (1961): structural identity for the summary table of average
    auction expectations. Column definitions:
      sellerReceipts = payment₁ + payment₂         (column 3 = column 1 + 2)
      totalValue     = sellerReceipts + netGain₁ + netGain₂  (column 6 = 3 + 4 + 5)
    The table identity asserts: totalValue = payment₁ + payment₂ + netGain₁ + netGain₂. -/
theorem Table_Vickrey3_p38_Summary
    (payment₁ payment₂ netGain₁ netGain₂ : ℝ) :
    let sellerReceipts := payment₁ + payment₂
    let totalValue := sellerReceipts + netGain₁ + netGain₂
    totalValue = payment₁ + payment₂ + netGain₁ + netGain₂ := by
  ring
